newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Time running out for Italy's troubled IRI.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Time running out for Italy's troubled IRI.

text.p: Time is running out for Italy's hugely indebted state holding company IRI but while the government wants a quick sell-off of assets, the group's top managers appear to be stalling.

IRI, set up by fascist dictator Benito Mussolini in 1933 to kick-start the country's industrialisation, is heading for huge losses this year and the government is now scrambling for ways to shore up the company's sagging balance sheet.

The group, which owns a clutch of key companies including state telecoms group Stet, engineering group Finmeccanica and state carrier Alitalia, is expected to lose up to three trillion lire ($2 billion) this year.

The government's biggest challenge now is how to cut IRI's 23.5 trillion lire gross debt mountain as fast as possible to stave off bankruptcy. But all is not well with the government's privatisation programme.

The sale of Stet, which controls Italy's main fixed line and mobile phone operators, ran into trouble on Tuesday when a parliamentary commission abandoned work on a watchdog body for the sector because of political filibustering.

The Treasury said on Wednesday it hoped Stet would be sold by the current deadline at the end of March 1997, so it can take advantage of a window of opportunity in Europe's busy privatisation programme.
"If this is not possible...the Stet sale will still go ahead in 1997, as soon as the watchdog authority is approved," the Treasury statement said.
As part of a 1993 deal, Italy has promised the European Union it will sell the huge telecoms group by next June.
Under the accord, IRI must cut its debt to below five trillion lire by the end of 1996. At the end of 1995, its net debt stood at 22.456 trillion lire.

Italian newspapers said the Treasury has devised plans to hive off IRI's most sellable assets such as Stet, Finmeccanica and toll-road operater Autostrade with the group's debts into a separate company.
That would leave IRI with the task of winding up the remaining activities that cannot be sold off to investors.
Francesco Giavazzi, an economic adviser to the treasury, said the sell-offs could be sped up if the treasury took direct control of IRI's most attractive assets.
IRI debts could also be converted into treasury instruments.

"The control of the treasury ministry over the companies that have to be privatised would be strengthened ... eliminating an intermediate level in the chain of command," said Giavazzi in a commentary in Milan's Corriere della Sera.
In a swipe at IRI top managers, who are openly opposing a break up of the group, Giavazzi said he did not see what role they had to play in privatising companies such as Stet.

"One can understand why the technicians of the (Stet) operating companies are invited to the table of the treasury minister, but one cannot see what role is played by the president and director general of IRI," he said.
IRI chairman Michele Tedeschi has rebuffed the plan to transfer his group's prize assets to the treasury, describing them as "a form of financial engineering."
Meanwhile, the treasury is considering a transfer to IRI of a company called Gepi in order to plug the hole in IRI's balance sheet, which will be left by this year's expected losses.
But the European Union's executive commission is believed to oppose the idea of the government recapitalising IRI by injecting fresh funds into the company.
